cases.rationale: White must manage the d4 passer and Black’s bishop pressure. The d-file blockade is durable, and the Rc7 and Bxd1 lines show a separate forcing exchange threat.
The central white knights can take on f6 and g7 in different orders and win h5. The alternative f3 plan avoids the exchange; durable strategic differences beyond the exposed king are less clear.

The knights and ...hxg3 expose the white king, with different exchanges in the leading lines. ...Rfc8 controls the open c-file and uses it in the forced rook exchange independently of which pawn capture comes first.
Several move orders create the same ...Ra3 and ...b5 plan. The a-file incursion and queenside pawn expansion matter even when the exchange on b4 changes order.
An advanced white rook is attacked from several directions. Rf8, Nxc7 and Be4+ lead to distinct concrete trades or threats, including skewer possibilities on the king.
Both ...Bd6 and the rook moves target the open e-file and shape pressure on White’s d5 passer. The resulting queen or bishop swaps leave a durable structural choice.
Black can reroute the bishop to e8, g4 or c8 while preparing to meet exd5. The isolated queenside pawns and opposing rook use of c-file pressure persist even after a central exchange.

...Qc7 and ...Qa7 answer the advanced white rook and produce a repeating threat. ...Rxa2 changes the immediate capture sequence. The strategic value of the doubled rooks beyond this defence remains unclear.
Rxc3 simply takes the exposed queen. The leading alternatives leave the queen free to move and lose the opportunity.
Rook checks require calculation after dxe6+ and Rxc8. Black’s a3 passer ties down White independently of the choice of exchange or check.
Black has to calculate around the rook on h7 and the f7 sacrifice. ...Rg7 and ...Rh8 lead to different forcing exchanges near the king.

...Bxf6 contests the f6 pawn and leaves a different h-file structure after gxh5. Dark-square pressure and the advanced pawn structure survive while both sides calculate the knight and bishop exchanges.
The h-pawn and the bishop on h6 create immediate checks and capture threats. ...h3 threatens hxg2, while ...Be3+ is much less effective against the waiting king retreat.
...Nf4+ and rook checks can sustain repetition. White’s doubled rooks and the d5/e4 pawns give separate durable incentives after a quiet king move.
White has to account for ...e3 and ...e2 in the concrete rook-exchange sequence. The e4 passer also restricts the king in the leading lines. The queenside pawn moves play against that confinement.
The active king, rook route and b-pawn promotion race govern the position. Several quiet approaches can reach comparable pressure without an urgent material tactic.
hxg6 and Rh1 create concrete forcing lines against the king. Black can use the c-file to trade for the bishop only through immediate exchanges. A separate durable gain is unclear.
Rxd1 and Bxc8 both need exact recapture and checking calculation against the exposed kings. The material snapshot alone cannot explain why both hold.
...f5 changes the direct attacking sequence. ...f6 allows Bxg6 hxg6 Qxg6+ and sustained checks from White.
...f5 and ...Be7 can transpose into the same defence against Qh6 and Ng5. ...Be8 gives White that attack with fewer effective replies.
Trading one knight changes White’s dark-square bishop and kingside pawn leverage. The best lines preserve different pawn structures around the open files, even with equal material.
...dxc4 takes the knight that White left on c4. The other leading candidates miss the concrete material opportunity.
The b7 bishop and d6 knight interact in concrete captures. ...Rc7 changes the recapture while White’s c-pawn and Black’s d-pawn remain long-term promotion threats.
The passed pawn can immediately take the c2 rook. ...Bd4+ changes the order, and ...Rxd8 takes the knight after the first exchange. The pawn is exchanged in those lines.
...Rae8 and ...Bd8 allow different forcing rook and queen routes against the white king. The relative contribution of a durable strategic advantage is unclear.
...Be7 develops to castle while ...Rc8 contests the c-file. The f4/e5 pawn tension and knight placement remain the main durable differences.
...c2 creates an immediate promotion threat. The queen moves fail to match that resource, and Qb2 permits a concrete capture and queening sequence.
White and Black contest the c-file around the c4 pawn. Rdc1 or Rc8 changes rook occupation, and the e5 pawn and black knight affect the pressure over several moves.
...dxe3 wins a bishop and creates an advanced e-pawn that reaches e2. ...Rxe3 takes the same bishop but leaves a less dangerous pawn structure.
...g5, ...gxf5 and ...b6 define different pawn structures and knight plans. The legal exchanges in the leading lines do not show a near-term forced material gain.
The b6 passer, dark-square pressure and black centre remain important after the queen and knight trades. Whether the check threats make this a tactical decision is uncertain.
Taking on b5 creates a distant passer while g3 or Rb2 favours rook pressure and king activation. The resulting rook and pawn roles are the durable contrast.

limitations: One engine-assisted reviewer examined the legal boards, leading lines and ordinary played-move probes before inspecting classifier outputs or optional position replies.

Tactical labels require a concrete material, mating or defensive calculation. Positional labels require an identifiable durable structure or activity consideration. Unknown denotes insufficient or ambiguous evidence.
Broadcast losses and controls were sampled in pairs from separate games within the two events. This stratification does not estimate prevalence across all classical positions.
The legacy position-character proxy scores a supported motif on the engine first choice and has no independent positional axis.
